blocks.title: Forms
blocks.md: **Oral literature** is composed and passed on by speech and performance, often with music and dance. Forms include **folktales** (often with animal or trickster characters), **myths**, **legends**, **proverbs**, **riddles**, **praise poems**, **songs**, **epics** and **lullabies**. It exists in many African languages and is still alive.

blocks.title: Functions and features
blocks.md: Oral literature **entertains**, **teaches** values, **preserves history**, praises or criticises leaders and marks events. Features of performance: a storyteller who uses voice, gesture and pace, **call and response** with the audience, repetition, songs inside the tale, formulaic openings and closings, and adaptation to each audience.

blocks.caption: Forms of oral literature and their purposes.
blocks.alt: A table of four oral forms and their purposes.

blocks.title: Oral and written
blocks.md: Oral works change with each telling and depend on memory and audience; written works are fixed on the page and can be read alone. Writers may draw on oral forms, using proverbs, folk-tale structure, rhythm and storytelling voice. Neither form is superior: each has its own strengths.

blocks.title: Respect and care
blocks.md:
- Do not call oral literature ‘primitive’: it is sophisticated art.
- Avoid generalising about ‘all Africa’: traditions differ by people and language.
- Always cite the community or storyteller when using a real tale; here the examples are original.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Analyse a folktale opening
blocks.statement: Original opening: ‘Listen, listen! Long ago, when the river still talked, there lived a tortoise who loved the drum more than his dinner.’ Identify oral features.
steps: ‘Listen, listen!’ is a call to the audience.
‘Long ago’ is a formulaic opening.
‘when the river still talked’ is fantasy/personification setting a magical world.
The tortoise trickster-type character suggests a moral tale.
blocks.answer: Audience address, formulaic opening, fantasy and a trickster-type character.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Function of a proverb
blocks.statement: Original proverb: ‘A hand that hides the seed cannot complain of an empty field.’ Explain its function.
steps: It uses a farming image to teach a moral lesson.
It means that someone who withholds effort or resources cannot blame the result.
Proverbs give short, memorable advice in speech.
blocks.answer: A short, vivid image teaching responsibility.

blocks.title: What is a context question?
blocks.md: A **context question** gives an extract and asks you to explain what is happening, where it occurs in the text, its **significance** and how the writer uses language. You show that you know both the extract and the whole work. In this pack we practise with original extracts; with a set text you use your own reading.

blocks.title: A four-part answer
blocks.md: 1. **Locate:** who is speaking, where in the text, what has just happened. 2. **Explain** what the extract says or shows. 3. **Analyse** language, form or technique with short quotations. 4. **Link** to a theme, a character’s development or what follows. Keep the answer proportionate to the marks.

blocks.caption: A four-part context answer.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: locate, explain, analyse and link.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Retelling the whole plot.
- Saying only ‘this shows the theme’ without explaining how.
- Forgetting to locate the extract.
- Quoting without comment.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Plan an answer
blocks.statement: Original extract from an imaginary novel: ‘Ndi folded the scholarship letter and slid it into his schoolbag. At supper he spoke only about football.’ Question: What does this extract show about Ndi? (4 marks)
steps: Locate: Ndi has just received a scholarship letter.
Explain: he hides the letter and avoids the subject.
Analyse: ‘slid’ and ‘spoke only about football’ suggest secrecy and avoidance.
Link: he may fear leaving home or disappointing his family; this may anticipate conflict.
blocks.answer: He hides important news; his behaviour suggests worry or divided loyalties.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Write the answer
blocks.statement: Write a model four-mark answer for the extract above.
steps: The extract shows Ndi concealing his scholarship letter from his family.
The verb ‘slid’ suggests secrecy, and ‘spoke only about football’ shows he is avoiding the subject.
This suggests that he is anxious about the opportunity, perhaps because it means leaving home.
The detail builds tension about the news that will have to come out.
blocks.answer: A concise answer: location, explanation, language, significance.

blocks.title: Unpack the question
blocks.md: Underline the **command words** (discuss, how far, to what extent, compare) and the **key terms** (for example ‘presentation of women’). Decide your **line of argument** in one sentence (the **thesis**). Note 3–4 points that support it and one complication or alternative view.

blocks.title: Paragraph structure
blocks.md: Each paragraph: **Point** (topic sentence), **Evidence** (short quotation or reference), **Explanation** (how it proves the point, with technique), **Link** (back to the question). Use connectives to move the argument along (‘furthermore’, ‘however’, ‘this suggests’). Keep a balance between plot and analysis.

items.text: Write paragraphs: point, evidence, explanation, link

blocks.caption: Essay planning steps.
blocks.alt: Four boxes in a chain from unpacking the question to a final judgement.

blocks.title: Opening and ending
blocks.md: The **introduction** answers the question directly and signals the line of argument; it does not retell the plot. The **conclusion** gives a reasoned judgement, ties the points together and avoids new evidence. Time: about 5 minutes planning, the rest writing and a final check.

blocks.title: Frequent errors
blocks.md:
- Writing everything known about a text instead of answering the question.
- Listing techniques without effects.
- No judgement in the conclusion.
- Unfinished essay: plan to finish.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Write a thesis
blocks.statement: Question: ‘Discuss the importance of setting in a story of your choice.’ Write a thesis for an imaginary story set in a village during a drought.
steps: Key terms: importance, setting.
Thesis: the drought setting is not just a backdrop but drives the characters’ choices and symbolises their struggle.
Plan: setting and mood; setting and conflict; setting and symbolism.
blocks.answer: A thesis linking setting to action and symbol.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Plan a paragraph
blocks.statement: Plan one paragraph for the thesis above: setting shaping choices.
steps: Point: the drought forces the villagers to choose between staying and leaving.
Evidence: short quotation about empty wells (imaginary).
Explanation: the image of dry wells shows lack of resources and pushes characters towards difficult decisions.
Link: so the setting directly shapes the plot.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original tale in outline: a hare refuses to share his harvest, then asks neighbours for help in a drought and is refused. Write a paragraph on the moral and the oral devices you would use in telling it.
exercises.model: The moral is that selfishness has consequences: those who refuse help cannot expect help. In telling the tale I would use repetition for each refusal, a refrain song the audience can join, vivid animal voices and a clear closing formula. Humour and a pause before the ending add suspense.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original extract: ‘The generator died. In the dark the family moved closer, and for once nobody reached for a phone.’ Write a short context-style comment on the effect of this moment.
exercises.model: The power cut removes the usual distractions. ‘Moved closer’ suggests a rediscovered closeness, and ‘for once’ implies that they are normally absorbed by phones. The moment may be used to show the value of simple family togetherness.
exercises.rubric: Situation (1); language (1); implication (1); link to theme (1).
exercises.explanation: The power cut removes the usual distractions. ‘Moved closer’ suggests a rediscovered closeness, and ‘for once’ implies that they are normally absorbed by phones. The moment may be used to show the value of simple family togetherness.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Original extract: ‘Auntie Mbong counted the notes twice and then once more, though the amount did not change.’ Explain what this reveals and how it might connect to the wider story.
exercises.model: The repeated counting shows anxiety and a lack of money; she hopes the amount will somehow grow. It reveals the tension of limited resources and may point to a decision she has to make, such as postponing a purchase or asking for help. In the wider story this might link to themes of economic pressure and family responsibility.
exercises.rubric: Meaning of repetition (1); emotion (1); link to theme/plot (2).
exercises.explanation: The repeated counting shows anxiety and a lack of money; she hopes the amount will somehow grow. It reveals the tension of limited resources and may point to a decision she has to make, such as postponing a purchase or asking for help. In the wider story this might link to themes of economic pressure and family responsibility.

exercises.prompt: Question: ‘How far is the opening of a novel important in establishing its themes?’ Write a one-sentence thesis and list two points.
exercises.model: Thesis: the opening is vital because it sets the tone and introduces the central tensions, though themes develop later. Points: (1) setting and atmosphere in the opening hint at themes; (2) introduction of a character’s conflict or desire.
exercises.rubric: Thesis (1); two relevant points (2); line to the question (1).
exercises.explanation: Thesis: the opening is vital because it sets the tone and introduces the central tensions, though themes develop later. Points: (1) setting and atmosphere in the opening hint at themes; (2) introduction of a character’s conflict or desire.

exercises.source: Original exercise written for CastBridge, in the style of the curriculum
exercises.prompt: Plan (not a full essay) for: ‘Compare the ways in which two poems present nature.’ Use two imaginary poems: one in which nature is peaceful, one in which it is threatening.
exercises.model: Introduction: both poems use nature to express human feelings but differ in tone. Para 1: imagery (soft, gentle verbs versus violent verbs). Para 2: form and sound (regular rhyme versus broken rhythm). Para 3: speaker’s attitude (comfort versus fear). Conclusion: the contrast shows nature as a mirror of human emotion.
exercises.rubric: Thesis (1); structured comparison (2); links to technique (1).
exercises.explanation: Introduction: both poems use nature to express human feelings but differ in tone. Para 1: imagery (soft, gentle verbs versus violent verbs). Para 2: form and sound (regular rhyme versus broken rhythm). Para 3: speaker’s attitude (comfort versus fear). Conclusion: the contrast shows nature as a mirror of human emotion.
